options: A named, reusable, parameterized chunk of Jinja — essentially a function for SQL
A special type of dbt test that only checks column types
A CSV file loaded via dbt seed
A YAML block that only configures materializations
questions.explain: A macro packages up Jinja logic once, with arguments, so it can be called by name from any model instead of being copy-pasted.

questions.q: Where do custom macros live in a dbt project, and how are they defined?
options: In the macros/ folder, using {% macro %} ... {% endmacro %}
In the seeds/ folder, using a CSV format
In dbt_project.yml directly, with no separate file needed
Macros cannot be defined by the user, only by dbt Labs
questions.explain: Macros are .sql files under macros/, defined with the {% macro name(args) %} ... {% endmacro %} block.

questions.q: Without `{{ return() }}`, what does calling a macro like `cents_to_dollars(...)` actually produce?
options: The rendered text between {% macro %} and {% endmacro %}, substituted directly into the SQL at the call site
Nothing — a macro without return() always compiles to an empty string
A compile-time error
A Python list by default
questions.explain: Without return(), a macro's rendered text itself is the output — Jinja substitutes the call with whatever text is inside the macro body.

questions.q: When should you use `{{ return(value) }}` inside a macro?
options: When the macro needs to hand back a real Python value, like a list or dict, rather than just rendered SQL text
It is required in every macro, with no exceptions
Only inside snapshot definitions
Only when calling a macro from another package
questions.explain: return() is for macros that compute and hand back an actual value (e.g. a list of statuses) to be used elsewhere, such as inside a for loop.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is writing a macro NOT worth it?
options: When it exists purely to hide a few lines of already-clear SQL behind a function call, making debugging harder for whoever reads it later
Whenever the same logic is used in three or more models
Whenever a default argument value is needed
Macros are always worth writing, with no exceptions
questions.explain: A macro used in only one model, wrapping straightforward SQL, adds indirection without the reuse benefit that justifies it — it becomes worth it once a second model needs the same logic.
